items.prose: On $X = \{a, b, c\}$ take $\tau = \{\varnothing, \{b\}, \{a, b\}, \{b, c\}, X\}$.
items.question: Is $\tau$ a topology?

options.text: Yes: $\{a, b\} \cap \{b, c\} = \{b\}$ and $\{a, b\} \cup \{b, c\} = X$ are members
No: the complement $\{a, c\}$ of $\{b\}$ is missing
options.why: Complements are not required; that is a $\sigma$-algebra rule.

feedback.correct: Right. It is the topology generated by $\{a, b\}$ and $\{b, c\}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check every union and intersection of two members.

explain.text: Every pair's union and intersection is a member, and $\varnothing$ and $X$ are in. This is the subbasis topology of l6.

items.prose: On $\{a, b, c\}$ take the basis $\{\{a\}, \{b, c\}\}$.
items.question: How many open sets does it generate, $\varnothing$ included?

feedback.generic: Not quite. List every union of pieces.

byKey.pieces: You counted the pieces. Their union $X$ and the empty union $\varnothing$ count too.

explain.text: The unions are $\varnothing$, $\{a\}$, $\{b, c\}$ and $X$: 4 open sets. This space is disconnected.

options.why: In $Y$ nothing lies above 1, so 1 needs no room on that side.

options.text: Yes, and so it is open in $\mathbb{R}$ too
options.why: $(0.5, 1]$ is not open in $\mathbb{R}$; openness in $Y$ does not carry up.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find an open $U$ of $\mathbb{R}$ with $U \cap Y = W$.

explain.text: $(0.5, 2)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}$ and meets $[0, 1]$ in $(0.5, 1]$. So $W$ is open in $Y$, though not in $\mathbb{R}$.

options.text: Removing 0 from $[0, 1]$ leaves it connected; removing any point of $(0, 1)$ does not
They have the same length, so nothing does
options.why: Length is a metric idea. Removing a point is a topological test, and it separates them.
Both are bounded. And boundedness is not kept by homeomorphisms anyway.

feedback.correct: Right. An end point survives its removal.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Remove a point from each and count pieces.

explain.text: $[0, 1] \setminus \{0\} = (0, 1]$ is connected. Every point of $(0, 1)$ splits it in two. A homeomorphism would keep this, so none exists.

items.prose: On $\{a, b, c\}$ take $\tau = \{\varnothing, \{a, b\}, \{c\}, X\}$.
items.question: Which pair separates the space?

options.text: No pair: the space is connected
options.why: $\{a, b\}$ and $\{c\}$ are open, disjoint, non-empty and cover $X$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Look for two open members that are complements.

explain.text: $\{a, b\}$ and $\{c\}$ are open complements of each other. So the space splits into the components $\{a, b\}$ and $\{c\}$.

items.prose: Let $S = \{0, 1\}$ be the Sierpiński space with $\{1\}$ open. Map $\mathbb{R}$ to $S$ by $f(x) = 1$ when $x > 0$ and $f(x) = 0$ otherwise.
items.question: Is $f$ continuous?

options.text: Yes: the preimages of $\varnothing$, $\{1\}$ and $S$ are $\varnothing$, $(0, \infty)$ and $\mathbb{R}$, all open

options.why: A jump matters only if some preimage fails. $\{0\}$ is not open in $S$, so its preimage need not be open.
$\{0\}$ is not an open set of $S$, so it is not tested.

feedback.correct: Right. Continuity depends on the target's open sets.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Test only the open sets of $S$.

explain.text: The open sets of $S$ are $\varnothing$, $\{1\}$ and $S$, with preimages $\varnothing$, $(0, \infty)$ and $\mathbb{R}$. All are open, so $f$ is continuous, jump and all.

items.prose: Hausdorff means any two distinct points have disjoint open sets round them.
items.question: Which spaces are Hausdorff? Select all that apply.

options.text: $\{a, b, c\}$ with the discrete topology

options.why: The only open set holding 0 is the whole space.
Any two non-empty open sets meet.
The only non-empty open set is $X$, holding both points.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Try to separate two points in each.

explain.text: Singletons separate points in a discrete space, and balls of radius $\tfrac{d(x, y)}{2}$ do in a metric space. In the other three, any two non-empty open sets meet.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use $|{-0.75}| = 0.75$ in the denominator.

byKey.inverse: You used the inverse $\tfrac{y}{1 + |y|}$. $f$ divides by $1 - |x|$.

items.prose: Let $D = [0, 1] \cup [2, 3]$ and $f : D \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f = 0$ on $[0, 1]$ and $f = 1$ on $[2, 3]$.
items.question: Is $f$ continuous, and does it take the value 0.5?

options.text: Continuous, and it misses 0.5: the intermediate value theorem needs a connected domain

options.why: You applied the theorem to a disconnected domain. $D$ splits into two open pieces, and $f$ is constant on each.

options.text: Not continuous, because it jumps from 0 to 1
options.why: There is no point where it jumps: $D$ has a gap between 1 and 2. Each preimage is open in $D$.

feedback.correct: Right. Connectedness is the hypothesis that matters.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check whether $D$ is connected.

explain.text: $[0, 1]$ and $[2, 3]$ are open in $D$, so $f$ is continuous. $D$ is disconnected, so its image $\{0, 1\}$ need not be an interval. The theorem needs a connected domain.
